title: The king
outcomes: Taps the squares a king can step to, never next to the enemy king or onto an attacked square
Knows the king can capture an enemy piece that is not protected
Says in a sentence why the king avoids attacked squares

steps.say: Move the king one square to the star.
Two squares away needs two steps.

steps.text: The king steps one square any way. It never steps next to the other king or onto a square an enemy piece attacks. It may capture an enemy piece, but only one that is not protected.

steps.say: You cannot step next to the other king. Find the way round.

steps.caption: The kings face each other with one square between. The three squares c4, d4 and e4 touch both kings, so the white king may not step there.

claims.statement: The white king can step to these five squares only.
The white king may not step to d4, next to the black king.

steps.say: Squares the bishop attacks are off limits. Find a safe path.
A knight attacks in L shapes, not diagonals. Find the safe route.
This knight is not protected. The king may take it.

steps.prompt: Say it back: how does the king move, where may it never go, and why?

steps.text: **Model answer.** The king steps one square in any direction. It never steps next to the other king, and never onto a square an enemy piece attacks, because a king there could be captured and a king may never be left to be captured. It may capture an enemy piece that is not protected.

sources: Rebuilt as a star-grab lesson on 8 Nov 2026 (docs/reach-step.md); wording original.
King movement and the forbidden squares are rules of the game; the board's squares are legal_destinations and illegal_move claims [V]. The idea of check is named elsewhere and not taught here [I].
Every reach round is solved by tools/validate_lessons.py (legal moves, par) [V]; the learning effect of moving first is a design bet [I].
